answers.question: List of scenarios
answers.answer: Arvida used three climate scenarios: (1) Hot House World (3.6°C by 2100), (2) Delayed and Disorderly (2.7°C by 2100), and (3) Ambitious and Orderly (1.4°C by 2100).

answers.question: Pick-and-mix of SSPs and RCPs
answers.answer: Arvida uses SSP-based scenarios (SSP1-1.9, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0) for their three narrative scenarios (Ambitious and Orderly, Delayed and Disorderly, Hot House World), while also referencing RCP 8.5 separately for physical risk assessments (e.g., designing new communities and assessing sea level rise under the Hot House World scenario).
answers.evidence: "Hot House World (<3°C) | Delayed and Disorderly | Ambitious and Orderly (>1.5°C) | Reference scenarios | SSP3-7 | SSP2-4.5 | SSP1-1.9" and "New communities are designed to withstand the extreme climate scenarios of RCP 8.5." and "The Company will continue to explore this further and consider a RCP 8.5 scenario."
answers.location_hint: Annual Report p.89 (scenario table), p.93 (physical risks table), p.94 (opportunities table)
answers.notes: Arvida's primary scenario framework uses SSPs (SSP1-1.9, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0) aligned to their three scenarios, but separately references RCP 8.5 for physical risk design standards and master planning — a classic pick-and-mix of SSP and RCP frameworks.

answers.question: Customised scenarios
answers.answer: Yes. Arvida developed customised scenarios by combining health sector scenarios (which Arvida jointly led) and property & construction sector scenarios (led by the New Zealand Green Building Council). These were applied together to develop Arvida's own scenarios, resulting in three named scenarios: "Ambitious and Orderly" (1.4°C by 2100), "Delayed and Disorderly," and "Hot House World."
answers.evidence: "This year, a focus for us was jointly leading the health sector to develop sector-level climate scenarios to assist the entire sector in understanding the potential impacts of climate change (both physical and transition) on population health and health service delivery... For our reporting this year, we have applied both the health sector and the property & construction sector scenarios to develop our own scenarios, which enabled us to carefully reconsider our climate-related risks and opportunities." and "and property sector scenarios, lead by the New Zealand Green Building Council last year, was used as these two sectors reflect the Company's business."
answers.notes: Arvida customised scenarios by combining health sector and property & construction sector scenarios. The three resulting scenarios are: Ambitious and Orderly (1.4°C), Delayed and Disorderly, and Hot House World.

answers.question: Co-produced climate scenarios
answers.answer: Yes. Arvida jointly led a project with Te Whatu Ora and around 30 other health sector participants to co-develop a set of sector-level climate scenarios, using consultants Tonkin + Taylor. Arvida's Head of Sustainability & Compliance chaired the Technical Working Group, and the GM Strategy was part of the leadership group. Through a series of workshops, the group developed three sector scenarios: a 1.5°C, a 2.7°C, and a 3.6°C scenario. Information from both the health sector work and the construction and property sector scenarios (led by the New Zealand Green Building Council) was then used to develop Arvida's own combined scenarios.
answers.evidence: The Company jointly led a project, with Te Whatu Ora and around 30 other health sector participants, to develop a set of sector scenarios with consultants Tonkin + Taylor. The Company's Head of Sustainability & Compliance was the Chair of the Technical Working Group and the Company's GM Strategy was part of the leadership group. Through a series of workshops, the group developed three sector scenarios. A 1.5°C, a 2.7°C and a 3.6°C scenario. In developing the Company's own scenarios, information from both the health sector work and the construction and property sector scenarios, lead by the New Zealand Green Building Council last year, was used as these two sectors reflect the Company's business.
answers.notes: The co-production involved Te Whatu Ora and ~30 other health sector participants, with Tonkin + Taylor as consultants. Arvida also drew on property & construction sector scenarios led by the NZ Green Building Council.

answers.question: Model used
answers.answer: A detailed emissions reduction model was developed and updated for the current year. The output demonstrates the relative merits and impacts of alternative sustainability initiatives in reducing Scope 1 and 2 emissions. For purchased goods and services (except food) and capital goods, emissions factors were sourced from Motu's "Consumption-based greenhouse gas emissions input-output model" (2013). For food, a New Zealand-based emissions model developed by Jonathan Drew ("Healthy and Climate-Friendly Eating Patterns in the New Zealand Context") was used.
answers.evidence:
"To help understand how to mitigate the Company's emissions, a detailed emissions reduction model has been developed and updated for the current year. The output from the model shown on page 43 demonstrates the relative merits and impacts of alternative sustainability initiatives in reducing Scope 1 and 2 emissions. The model has allowed the most effective emission reduction targets to be identified."

"The emissions factors for purchased goods and services (except food) and capital goods have been sourced from Motu and are adjusted for inflation to 2007 when the research was conducted."

"The emissions factors for food are based on the work of Jonathan Drew who developed a New Zealand based emissions model which differentiated emissions from both New Zealand food supply and production. Using the 'Healthy and Climate-Friendly Eating Patterns in the New Zealand Context' database developed by Drew and updated by Auckland University, the appropriate emission factors were allocated to each ingredient."
answers.location_hint: Annual Report p.95; Emissions Inventory Report p.6
answers.notes: The question "Model used" is somewhat ambiguous — it could refer to the emissions reduction model, the GHG inventory calculation model, or the climate scenario model. The context references multiple models: (1) an internal emissions reduction model for Scope 1 & 2, (2) Motu's input-output model for purchased goods/services EFs, and (3) Drew's NZ food emissions model. All are directly stated in the context.

answers.question: Damage from acute physical risk considered
answers.answer: Yes. Arvida considers damage from acute physical risks including extreme weather events (storms, floods, wildfires). Specific examples include: (1) The January 2023 Auckland flooding caused extensive damage to 39 villas and the Community Centre and Serviced Apartments building at Parklane, with a material damage insurance settlement of $14.9 million; (2) Cyclone Gabrielle impacted northern regions; (3) Port Hills wildfires in February 2024 required resident evacuation. Anticipated impacts include increased capital costs associated with material damage to assets and increased operational costs associated with repairs and/or increased insurance premiums.
answers.evidence: "Extreme weather events may result in increased capital costs associated with material damage to Arvida's assets and/or additional mitigation or adaptation measures. Also, there are increased operational costs associated with repairs and/or increased insurance premiums and/or disruption to supply chains." and "On 27 January 2023, a weather event in Auckland resulted in serious flooding occurring in part of the Group's Parklane retirement community. The flooding caused extensive damage to 39 villas and the Community Centre and Serviced Apartments building... On 2 August 2023, the Group settled the material damage claim with insurers for the flooding event at Parklane for $14.9m."
answers.location_hint: Page 93 (risk table), Page 68 (insurance receivable note), Page 88 (current climate-related impacts)
answers.notes: Arvida explicitly identifies extreme weather events (storms, floods, wildfires) as acute physical risks and has experienced actual material damage from the 2023 Auckland floods ($14.9m settlement) and indirect impacts from Cyclone Gabrielle and Port Hills wildfires.

answers.question: Time frames
answers.answer:
Arvida uses three time frames:
- Short term (S): 0–3 years — Construction timeframe for a stage in a retirement community, from project inception, planning and resource allocation, through to completion and occupation by residents.
- Medium term (M): 3–10 years — Estimated duration to develop a retirement village and the average tenure of an independent resident (8–9 years) living in the Company's retirement communities.
- Long term (L): 10–30 years — Total useful life of a building or retirement community. However, the ability to modify and adjust several aspects, as part of refurbishments and regular maintenance, is a key factor in reducing the long-term timeframe.

answers.question: Justification for scenario/model choice
answers.answer: Arvida chose scenarios based on two sector-specific sources: (1) health sector scenarios developed jointly with Te Whatu Ora and ~30 other health sector participants (consultants Tonkin + Taylor), producing 1.5°C, 2.7°C, and 3.6°C scenarios; and (2) property & construction sector scenarios led by the New Zealand Green Building Council. These two sectors were selected because they reflect the Company's business. The reference scenarios are SSP1-1.9 (1.4°C), SSP2-4.5 (2.7°C), and SSP3-7 (3.6°C).

The health sector scenarios were developed collaboratively with Te Whatu Ora and ~30 other participants using Tonkin + Taylor as consultants.

answers.question: Historic climate impacts
answers.answer:
Arvida experienced several historic climate impacts:

1. **January 2023 Auckland flooding**: A significant rain event caused widespread flooding, resulting in the flooding of one Auckland village. The final settlement for the material damage insurance claim was $14.9 million, with $9.2 million received in FY24. Court proceedings were also filed against insurers (QBE and IAG) regarding the business interruption claim.

2. **Cyclone Gabrielle (February 2023)**: Impacted northern regions of New Zealand including Hawke's Bay. While Arvida's Mary Doyle community did not experience material damage, widespread regional damage caused shortages of qualified nursing staff, leading to closure of a number of care beds, a revenue reduction of $1.6m, reduced profitability, and a reduction to care asset valuation of $0.9m.

3. **Port Hills wildfires (February 2024)**: Arvida's Rhodes on Cashmere community was some distance from the fire with no material damage, but a number of residents were evacuated as a precaution. The incident tested the Company's emergency and crisis management plans.
answers.evidence: "During 2023, two severe weather events occurred: a significant rain event in late January 2023 that caused widespread flooding in Auckland; and, shortly thereafter, cyclone Gabrielle that affected eastern and coastal regions in the North Island... The final settlement for the material damage component of the insurance claim was $14.9 million with $9.2 million received in FY24. In FY23 cyclone Gabrielle significantly impacted northern regions of New Zealand, including the Hawke's Bay region. Mary Doyle, our community in the region, did not experience any material damage related to the cyclone. However, the widespread damage to the region from the cyclone has resulted in shortages of qualified nursing staff. This has resulted in the Company closing a number of beds in the care facility and a reduction in revenue of $1.6m, reduced profitability and a reduction to care asset valuation of $0.9m... The Company was also impacted by the Port Hills wildfires in February 2024. While our community (Rhodes on Cashmere) was some distance from the fire, and there was no material damage, a number of residents were evacuated as a precaution."
answers.notes: All three climate events and their financial/operational impacts are explicitly described in the document.

answers.question: Direct and indirect physical climate risks
answers.answer:
Arvida identifies the following direct and indirect physical climate risks:

1. **Extreme weather events (storms, floods, wildfires)** [Short, Medium & Long term]: May result in increased capital costs from material damage to assets and/or additional mitigation/adaptation measures, increased operational costs from repairs, increased insurance premiums, and disruption to supply chains.

2. **Sea level rise** [Long term]: May result in managed retreat from coastal locations, stranded assets, and increased capital costs associated with managing fluvial floods. Further assessment indicates no communities are at risk under the Hot House World scenario within short-, medium-, or long-term horizons to 2055.

3. **Rising temperatures** [Medium & Long term]: May result in increased operational costs due to demand for air conditioning systems and/or increased illness in residents, and increased capital costs associated with air conditioning systems.

Real-world examples of physical climate impacts already experienced include:
- Flooding of an Auckland village (January 2023 rain event), with a final material damage insurance settlement of $14.9 million ($9.2 million received in FY24) and an ongoing business interruption claim against QBE and IAG.
- Cyclone Gabrielle (FY23) caused nursing staff shortages at Mary Doyle community in Hawke's Bay, leading to bed closures, a revenue reduction of $1.6m, reduced profitability, and a care asset valuation reduction of $0.9m.
- Port Hills wildfires (February 2024) required precautionary evacuation of residents at Rhodes on Cashmere community, with no material damage but significant disruption.
answers.evidence: Extreme weather events may result in increased capital costs associated with material damage to Arvida's assets and/or additional mitigation or adaptation measures. Also, there are increased operational costs associated with repairs and/or increased insurance premiums and/or disruption to supply chains... Sea level rise may result in managed retreat from coastal locations and may result in assets that become stranded. It may result in increased capital costs associated with managing fluvial floods. Further work has been done to assess the risk of sea level rise at our communities and indicates there are no communities at risk under the Hot House World scenario under Arvida's short-, medium-, or long-term time horizons to 2055... Extreme temperatures may result in increased operational costs, as a result of demand for air conditioning systems and/or increased illness in our residents. Also, there are increased capital costs associated with air conditioning systems in our communities... While the Company has concluded and settled its material damages claim in relation to the flooding of one of its Auckland villages, court proceedings have been filed against its insurers – QBE and IAG – in relation to resolving the business interruption claim... The final settlement for the material damage component of the insurance claim was $14.9 million with $9.2 million received in FY24... the widespread damage to the region from the cyclone has resulted in shortages of qualified nursing staff. This has resulted in the Company closing a number of beds in the care facility and a reduction in revenue of $1.6m, reduced profitability and a reduction to care asset valuation of $0.9m... The Company was also impacted by the Port Hills wildfires in February 2024. While our community (Rhodes on Cashmere) was some distance from the fire, and there was no material damage, a number of residents were evacuated as a precaution.
answers.notes: The document distinguishes between direct physical risks (damage to assets from extreme weather, sea level rise, rising temperatures) and indirect physical risks (e.g., nursing staff shortages due to regional cyclone damage). All risks are explicitly stated in the climate disclosures section.
